scopeNotes: New text needs independent review; earlier hashes do not certify it.
Map endpoints are not historical founding or extinction dates.

The 1650 to 1715 and 1878 to present records are associated geographically, not merged as one uninterrupted state. Their gap is not a historical extinction. The imported polygons are not newly certified and no successor links are added.

Maya sites precede the selected opening period. The 600 to 900 phase is a broad Classic-period window; Ta’ab Nuk Na Building B is more narrowly dated to approximately 650 to 780. Lamanai’s long occupation is a separate site history, not evidence that salt production continued indefinitely.

Ta’ab Nuk Na household activities are inferred from excavated objects and their distribution. The whistle’s possible Lubaantun origin does not identify its user; musical occasion is unknown. A small stirring paddle at this site is not confused with the canoe paddle from another Paynes Creek site.

The 1544 opening marks a selected mission phase at Lamanai, not conquest of the entire mapped region or the beginning of British timber extraction. Courtyard teaching is Graham’s comparative interpretation. No claim of voluntary conversion or a specific pupil’s experience is made.

Palacio’s community account is used for contemporary food knowledge and the 1862/1871 institutional distinction. Its broad prehistoric migration chronology, sweeping cultural origin accounts and transatlantic-slavery totals are not adopted. The child’s activity is identified by the author’s printed caption; no personal identity, family relationship or universal childcare rule is inferred.

The consular overview calls 1862 crown colony status, whereas Palacio distinguishes formal colony in 1862 from crown colony government in 1871. The card preserves the latter distinction. The consulate’s 1502 and 1638 arrival claims, 1840 terminology, earliest-population assertion and language stereotypes are not used.

The 2013 report reviewed in 2014 is available as an English summary on UNESCO’s Spanish-language state page. It spells the school Guilisi; the card uses the Gulisi spelling in other institutional records. Teaching is attributed to that report, and the 2011 date concerns the new building. Neither medical effectiveness nor current programme availability is inferred.

The former-hospital page timed out on direct access but its relevant full text was available in an indexed result. The UNESCO summary was likewise read in indexed form. The official parliamentary constitution PDF confirmed the independence date in its indexed text, but direct access led to a suspended-host page. It is omitted from reader links in favour of the accessible consular account.
This regional card does not exhaust every community in Belize. Garifuna, Maya and Kriol examples retain their local identities and dates rather than being presented as one shared custom.
New prose has been checked by its author against the cited passages and awaits independent historical review.

identityEvidence.assessment: Geographic identity agrees along the Caribbean coast south of Mexico. Near-identical historical bounds do not prove seventeenth-century British sovereignty over modern Belize. Snapshot dates remain unchanged and explicitly represent coverage.

sharedAssociations.basis: Decoded 1650 and 1878 outlines occupy the same Belize region; see identityEvidence. One geographic narrative spans distinct Maya, colonial and independent periods, without certifying colonial control over the imported full outline.
